title: Reliable Probabilistic Forecasting of Irregular Time Series through Marginalization-Consistent Flows
one_liner: A method that forecasts multiple time series together while guaranteeing that individual forecasts match what you'd predict alone.
lead: When you forecast multiple related time series at once (like stock price and trading volume), the model learns a joint pattern. But here is the problem: the predictions for each series individually can violate what the model itself predicts when asked about that series in isolation. MOSES fixes this by designing the forecasting model to be analytically marginalized—meaning individual predictions are mathematically guaranteed to come from the same model as the joint forecast.

problem.h2: The consistency trap in joint forecasting
paras: When a forecasting model learns patterns in multiple related time series (like temperature and humidity), it learns how they move together. A naive approach: train one model on all the series at once, then use it to answer both 'joint' questions ('what are temperature and humidity together?') and 'marginal' questions ('what is just temperature?'). This seems logical but it breaks in a subtle way.

The issue is that the model's answers to single-series questions do not match what the model predicts when you ask it about that series in isolation. Imagine the model forecasts joint temperature-humidity as a cloud of possibilities. When you extract just temperature from that cloud, the resulting temperature predictions are not the same as what the model would produce if trained to forecast temperature alone. This inconsistency makes individual predictions unreliable and harder to interpret.

callout.html: Standard forecasting models make joint and marginal predictions that contradict each other, destroying trust in individual predictions.

steps.b: Define the model as a mixture
steps.text: Start with K mixture components, each a normalizing flow (a learnable transformation).

steps.b: Separate the core and the details
steps.text: Each component has one shared latent Gaussian (the backbone) and one separate univariate transformation per variable.
Learn the shared backbone and separate paths from examples of all variables together.
Drop a variable and integrate it out mathematically; no sampling, no approximation.
Both joint and marginal predictions come from the same model by design, not chance.

paras: MOSES changes how the model is built, not what it predicts. Specifically, it parametrizes the normalizing flow—the learned transformation that converts random noise into realistic predictions—using a separable structure: a shared multivariate core and independent univariate paths for each variable.

hidden.name: consistency between joint and marginal predictions
paras: Marginalization consistency is a check: when you remove a variable from the model's joint prediction, does the set of predictions for the remaining variables match what the model predicts when asked about those variables alone? In a consistent model, yes. In an inconsistent model, no. MOSES measures this by literally extracting the marginal (mathematically integrating out the removed variable) and comparing it to a single-variable forecast.

The paper estimates this consistency by computing log-likelihood on held-out test data. If the model is truly consistent, log-likelihood for individual variables should equal the likelihood of those variables extracted from the joint—they are the same object. MOSES achieves this by design: separable flows guarantee that marginals are always mathematically exact, never approximated.

heat.caption: Darker means more relevant to consistency. Highlight boxes show the check: marginal from joint must match temp-alone model.

reads.html: A model is marginalization-consistent if predictions for a single variable, extracted from a joint forecast, match what you'd get forecasting that variable on its own.
Marginalization consistency: for any subset S of variables, the marginal (computed by integrating out unwanted variables from the joint) equals the model's direct forecast for S alone.

paras: Here is why it works: if you design the model so that each variable has its own transformation path that does not interact with others (separable), then dropping a variable is just like never running that path. Mathematically, integrating out that variable gives you exactly the original model for the remaining variables. No contradiction, no approximation.

Technically, MOSES represents each component of the mixture as: a shared multivariate Gaussian (the latent backbone, shared across all variables), plus one univariate transformation (a normalizing flow) per variable that acts independently on its channel. When you want the marginal for a subset of variables, you integrate out the unwanted ones analytically. Because the shared backbone is Gaussian and the unwanted transformations are independent, integration is exact and closed-form. You never lose information or introduce inconsistency.

Why this works in practice: normalizing flows are flexible models that can learn many different shapes. By layering them (K mixture components), MOSES can learn complex joint patterns. The separable structure does not lose expressiveness for the joint—it only enforces a constraint that makes marginals reliable. In tests, MOSES achieves near-optimal joint predictions while guaranteeing marginal correctness.

stages.s: Multivariate irregular time series (missing values, different lengths)
Apply univariate normalizing flow per variable (temperature path, humidity path, etc.)
Mixture of K components (each a backbone + set of paths)
For joint forecast: sample all variables. For marginal: integrate out unwanted paths analytically.
Reliable joint and marginal probabilistic forecasts

math.words: The model is a mixture of normalizing flows. Each component combines a shared latent Gaussian density with independent univariate transformations. For each component k, the density factors as: the Gaussian density times the product of univariate transformations (one per variable), adjusted for volume changes during transformation.
math.equation: p(x_1, ..., x_n | k) = N(z; mu_k, Sigma_k) * prod_i det(dT_i/dz_i) * prod_i p_i(T_i(z_i))
symbols: the shared latent Gaussian random vector (the backbone)
Gaussian density for component k with mean mu_k and covariance Sigma_k
univariate normalizing flow for variable i (transforms latent to observation)
volume change factor for transformation i (Jacobian determinant)
the target univariate distribution for variable i (learned)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose two variables (temperature, humidity), 3 mixture components, shared latent z is 2D Gaussian.
Temp path: T_1(z_1) = z_1^2 + 0.5, volume change = 2*z_1. Humid path: T_2(z_2) = exp(z_2), volume change = exp(z_2).
Joint density at sample (temp=1.5, humid=2.0) = Gaussian_1(z*) * 2*z_1* * exp(z_2*) * p_1(1.5) * p_2(2.0) where z* solves T_1(z_1*)=1.5, T_2(z_2*)=2.0.

Marginal for temperature: integrate humidity out. Since humid transform is independent, integration simplifies. Result: p(temp) depends only on temp-path, not humid-path—consistent with single-variable model.

math.note: The factorization into independent paths forces margins to be extractable exactly, avoiding the contradiction between joint and marginal predictions.

bars.h2: Accuracy on joint and marginal forecasts

charts.title: Standard flow model (ProFITi-like)
charts.note: High joint accuracy but individual-variable forecasts are unreliable; model contradicts itself.

charts.title: MOSES (separable flow)
charts.note: Slightly lower joint (cost of separability) but marginals are rock-solid and perfectly consistent with joint. Trust in individual predictions is restored.

items.html: If the joint distribution has very complex correlations between variables (not captured by a shared Gaussian backbone), separable flows may not fit the joint as tightly as a fully expressive unrestricted flow. MOSES is designed to sacrifice some joint fit for marginal correctness.

items.b: Irregular sampling and missing data require careful handling.
items.html: Real time series have gaps, irregular spacing, and missing values. MOSES must interpolate or encode these gaps into the model. If encoding is poor, both joint and marginal forecasts degrade.

items.b: Mixture size K must be chosen carefully.
items.html: Too few components underfits; too many causes overfitting. The number of components controls expressiveness of the joint distribution, so K must be tuned for each dataset.

MOSES delivers marginally consistent predictions on irregular time series, trading small joint accuracy loss for reliable, truthful individual forecasts. This is the intended design: you accept slightly less joint fit in exchange for predictions you can trust and interpret.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic dataset: two time series with known correlation (e.g., sales and inventory, or temperature and power demand). Train MOSES and a baseline (unrestricted normalizing flow like ProFITi) on joint data. Then generate three sets of predictions: (1) joint forecast for both variables, (2) marginal forecast extracted from the joint, (3) single-variable forecast for each variable trained on that variable alone. Compute log-likelihood for each variable in all three settings. The demo must show that MOSES marginals (set 2) have log-likelihood very close to single-variable forecasts (set 3), while the baseline marginals diverge sharply from single-variable truth.
demo.closing: MOSES makes consistency_loss near zero; standard flows make it large. This gap is impossible to miss and proves the method works.
